title: Rating, ranking, and understanding acoustical quality in university classrooms
research_question: To rate, rank, and understand the acoustical quality in 279 university classrooms at the University of British Columbia (UBC) for unaided speech, and to identify factors leading to best and worst conditions.

participants.description: University classrooms at the University of British Columbia (UBC), Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada. The study predicts speech intelligibility for 'average, normal-hearing listeners working in their first language.'
participants.recruitment: All unrestricted-access university classrooms at UBC were included.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: 279 existing university classrooms at UBC, characterized by their physical dimensions (length, width, height, volume, floor area, capacity) and acoustical properties (surface absorption coefficient, ventilation noise levels).

measures.instrument: Predicted from Speech Transmission Index (STI) using a regression equation (Barnett and Knight, 1995)
Calculated from Speech-signal to background-noise level difference (SNA) and 1 kHz Early Decay Time (EDT1) using Steeneken and Houtgast (1980) procedure
Calculated from A-weighted speech level (SLA) and A-weighted background-noise level (BGNA)
Calculated as energetic sum of A-weighted ventilation noise (VNA) and A-weighted student-activity noise (SANA)
Measured at two to four typical positions in unoccupied classrooms
Predicted using empirical formulas (Hodgson et al., 1999)
Measured in 76 classrooms, predicted for others using empirical method
Measured (length, width, height, volume, floor area)
Varied in prediction (Loud male, Average male, Average female, Quiet female)

mechanisms: Speech Intelligibility (SI) is predicted from Speech Transmission Index (STI), which is determined by the speech-signal to background-noise level difference (SNA) and early decay time (EDT1). These physical parameters directly influence the clarity and audibility of speech, which are critical for cognitive processing and understanding. A clear acoustic signal (high SNA, appropriate EDT1) reduces cognitive load for listeners, allowing for better speech perception and learning.
implementation_implications: New classroom acoustical design and renovation should prioritize limiting background noise.
Design should promote high instructor speech levels, especially at the back of classrooms.

Limiting the amount of sound absorption to control reverberation should be considered, but reverberation control for its own sake is not a primary design priority as speech quality is not highly sensitive to it.
High speech quality can be achieved in classrooms of any size if they are well designed.
Speech-reinforcement systems are generally not necessary for speakers with typical or strong voices.
Speech-reinforcement systems can be beneficial for increasing instructor speech levels, particularly at the back of the classroom or for quiet instructors.

limitations: The study relies on empirical models and a simplified STI-calculation procedure, which need to be validated experimentally in future work.
Noise from in-class equipment and outside the classroom was assumed negligible.
Diffuse-field theory was used to correct unoccupied SLA to occupied conditions, despite its known inaccuracy for steady-state levels, due to lack of a better method.

A-weighted ventilation-noise levels were measured at a few typical positions and are indicative, not precise, as actual levels can vary with system condition (air filters, blockages) and type (constant-air-volume vs. variable-air-volume systems).
The univariate analysis of factors affecting quality ignores possible interactions between parameters.

paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Nonoptimal classroom acoustical conditions directly affect speech perception and, thus, learning by students. Moreover, they may lead to voice problems for the instructor, who is forced to raise his/her voice when lecturing to compensate for poor acoustical conditions. The project applied previously developed simplified methods to predict speech intelligibility in occupied classrooms from measurements in unoccupied and occupied university classrooms. The methods were used to predict the speech intelligibility at various positions in 279 University of British Columbia (UBC) classrooms, when 70% occupied, and for four instructor voice levels. Classrooms were classified and rank ordered by acoustical quality, as determined by the room-average speech intelligibility. This information was used by UBC to prioritize classrooms for renovation. Here, the statistical results are reported to illustrate the range of acoustical qualities found at a typical university. Moreover, the variations of quality with relevant classroom acoustical parameters were studied to better understand the results. In particular, the factors leading to the best and worst conditions were studied. It was found that 81% of the 279 classrooms have “good,” “very good,” or “excellent” acoustical quality with a “typical” (average-male) instructor. However, 50 (18%) of the classrooms had “fair” or “poor” quality, and two had “bad” quality, due to high ventilation-noise levels. Most rooms were “very good” or “excellent” at the front, and “good” or “very good” at the back. Speech quality varied strongly with the instructor voice level. In the worst case considered, with a quiet female instructor, most of the classrooms were “bad” or “poor.” Quality also varies with occupancy, with decreased occupancy resulting in decreased quality. The research showed that a new classroom acoustical design and renovation should focus on limiting background noise. They should promote high instructor speech levels at the back of the classrooms. This involves, in part, limiting the amount of sound absorption that is introduced into classrooms to control reverberation. Speech quality is not very sensitive to changes in reverberation, so controlling it for its own sake should not be a design priority.
